chunks: Yūnus, from some of his companions, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

If a man strikes another man with a staff or with a stone, and he dies from a single blow before speaking, then it is quasi-intentional killing, and the diyyah is upon the killer. But if he repeatedly struck him and persisted against him with the staff or stones until he killed him, then it is intentional killing, and he is to be killed for it. And if he struck him a single blow, and he spoke, then remained for a day or more than a day, then died, then it is quasi-intentional killing.

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: The prescribed blood-money compensation owed for unlawful killing.
key_terms.الْعَصَا: A staff or stick used as the striking instrument.
key_terms.الْقَاتِلِ: The killer, upon whom liability falls in this ruling.
key_terms.شَبِيهُ الْعَمْدِ: Quasi-intentional killing; a category resembling intentional homicide but carrying diyyah rather than qisas in this context.
key_terms.عَمْدٌ: Intentional killing done deliberately in a manner establishing qisas.
key_terms.يُقْتَلُ بِهِ: He is killed for it; retaliation applies against the perpetrator.

ai.seo_question: When is a killing with a stick or stone considered intentional or quasi-intentional in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith explains legal distinctions between quasi-intentional and intentional killing in cases of assault with a staff or stones. It outlines when retaliation applies and when diyyah is due, based on the nature of the assault and the victim’s condition after the blow.
